question: On 31 August 2026, Greece signed an agreement (dubbed ‘Achilles’ Shield’) with Israel worth around EUR 3 billion for the purchase of an integrated anti-missile and anti-drone defence system, produced by Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries, plus EUR 26 million for an additional anti-drone system. This is the largest defence contract between the two countries.

Greece is a beneficiary of the SAFE instrument (Regulation (EU) 2025/1106), which imposes eligibility requirements regarding the origin of contractors and components. It should also be kept in mind that Israel is subject to genocide proceedings before the International Court of Justice and that several Member States have suspended trade in military material with Israel. In light of the above: 1.

Is the purchase of ‘Achilles’ Shield’ fully or partially financed, co-financed or otherwise supported by SAFE, the European Defence Industry Programme, the European Defence Fund or any other EU instrument?
Has the Commission checked that the SAFE eligibility requirements, including the limit for components originating from third countries, were met in the Greek contracts covered by the instrument?
What monitoring mechanisms ensure that EU funds or loans are not used, directly or indirectly, for purchasing material from Israeli companies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.11.2026) Under the Security Action for Europe Regulation1, contractors and subcontractors shall be established and have their executive management structures in the EU, EEA2 EFTA3 States or Ukraine. Entities established in Canada are also eligible to participate pursuant to the Agreement between the EU and Canada4.

The cost of components originating in countries other than the EU, EEA EFTA States or Ukraine shall not exceed 35% of the total cost of the components of the end product. The Commission assesses the eligibility of procurements included in the national defence investment plans. Disbursements are linked to the fulfilment of the conditions set out in the operational arrangements.

Member States will have to provide evidence on the compatibility with the eligibility rules and will regularly report on the implementation of their national defence investment plans. The European Defence Industry Programme5 contains comparable eligibility conditions.

The European Defence Fund6 is a grant’s scheme programme supporting collaborative research and development projects among Member States’ defence industry with similar eligibility rules for the participation of entities.

Under these EU programmes, eligibility is in principle limited to entities established in the EU, in Ukraine or in EEA EFTA States, provided that those entities are not controlled by third countries and third country entities.

By way of exception, entities established in the EU, in Ukraine or in an EEA EFTA State but controlled by a third country or third country entity could participate in the common procurements subject to the safeguards and conditions set out in the relevant EU instrument.

All these instruments refer to the standard competences of the European Anti-Fraud Office, the European Court of Auditors and the European Public Prosecutor's Office to perform their duties for the protection of the financial interests of the EU.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/1106/oj/eng/pdf. 2 European Economic Area. 3 European Free Trade Association. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2026/445/oj. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/2643/oj/eng. 6 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/697/oj/eng.
